issues.issue: The definition sweeps in "leases, and other title exceptions and encumbrances affecting Real Property," so ordinary easements and leases are "Liens" for purposes of the Section 7.2 blanket prohibition. Permitted Liens clause (k) excuses easements only for Real Property, leaving other title exceptions technically prohibited.

After a closed list of named documents, the definition adds "any other agreement entered into, now or in the future, by any Borrower and Lender in connection with this Agreement." How far that general catch-all reaches beyond the enumerated instruments is left open, and defaults under "Loan Documents" are Events of Default.

"Material adverse change in the business, prospects, operations, results of operations, assets, liabilities or financial condition" turns on the undefined words "material" and, notably, "prospects," with no baseline or threshold given. The term gates Section 3.3(d) advances and Section 8.9, so its boundary is squarely operative.

A $50,000,000 facility cannot be drawn without breaching Section 7.16(b), which caps the Senior Leverage Ratio (Obligations over Tangible Net Worth) at 0.9% while Section 7.16(a) sets minimum Tangible Net Worth at $600,000,000 — a ceiling of roughly $5.4 million of Obligations. The stated commitment and the financial covenant cannot both be given effect.

The parenthetical "(less portions that are not in compliance with the definition thereof)" subtracts from an aggregate that, by definition, already excludes non-complying notes. Whether it is surplusage or a second haircut is unclear.

The definition dates the test from "after the Effective Date," but "Effective Date" is not a defined term anywhere in this Agreement, which uses "Closing Date" throughout (including in the parallel carve-out in the "Subsidiary" definition). The date from which an entity qualifies as a New Fund is therefore unfixed.

The definition requires a Lien on "real property owned by the maker of such note," which by its terms excludes any loan secured by property owned by a third party or an affiliate of the maker. Whether such loans are Notes Receivable at all — and so part of the collateral and Borrowing Base — is contestable.

"A determination made in the exercise of reasonable (from the perspective of a secured asset-based lender) business judgment" fuses an objective reasonableness test with a partisan point of view, and gives no benchmark. Nearly every discretionary Lender act in the Agreement is measured by it.

Clause (c) permits "the use or transfer of money or Cash Equivalents in a manner that is not prohibited by the terms of this Agreement" — a circular catch-all sitting alongside six tightly specified dispositions, so its reach is set only by whatever else the Agreement happens not to forbid. Clause (e) compounds this by permitting sales of Notes Receivable "for a cash purchase price of not less than eighty (80%) of the unpaid balance," a figure whose unit is left out.

Section 4.1 states that "except for Permitted Dispositions, Borrowers and their Subsidiaries shall have no authority, express or implied, to dispose of any item or portion of the Collateral," and Sections 7.3(c) and 7.4 rest on the same carve-out. A broad reading of this definition would swallow those prohibitions and let the Borrowers release collateral at will.

Clause (c) reads "so long as such Liens for Approved Debt or subordinated to the Liens held by Lender on the terms approved by Lender" — the word "are" is missing, so the condition on which Approved Debt liens qualify as Permitted Liens is grammatically incoherent. Clause (e) also refers to Liens securing "Purchase Money Indebtedness" and then conditions them on securing "Permitted Purchase Money Indebtedness."

Condition (a) requires the reorganization to be "consistent in all material respects with the written description provided to Lender by Borrowers prior to the Closing Date," an extrinsic document neither attached nor described. What the Permitted Reorganization actually authorises therefore cannot be determined from the instrument.

Real Estate Owned is treated throughout as collateral — it is listed on the Borrowing Base Certificate and its sale is a Permitted Disposition — yet the "Borrower Collateral" definition does not enumerate Real Property among the granted categories. The two provisions leave the status of foreclosed real estate unsettled.

Clause (d) defines a Restricted Payment as a payment on Subordinated Debt or holder Indebtedness "to the extent such action would cause an Event of Default to occur hereunder," which is circular because Section 7.10's prohibition on Restricted Payments is itself what creates the Event of Default. Clause (e) then adds a residual for any payment "not expressly authorized in this Agreement."

The ratio is Obligations over Tangible Net Worth, and Section 7.16(b) caps it at 0.9% "expressed as a percentage"; with the $600,000,000 minimum Tangible Net Worth required by Section 7.16(a), that permits only about $5.4 million of Obligations against a $50,000,000 Maximum Revolver Amount. The definition and the covenant cannot be harmonised with the facility size.

"Solvent" is given a bare balance-sheet meaning — "at fair valuations, the sum of such Person's assets is greater than all of such Person's debts" — with no definition of "debts" (contingent, disputed, subordinated?) and none of the customary capital-adequacy or ability-to-pay prongs. Since Section 5.12 is captioned "Fraudulent Transfer," the gap between this test and the statutory ones is exactly what a court would have to construe.
